stimulus.source_note: Original secondary account drawn from the grounding books and verified against the books' own figures: student strikes at San Francisco State University in 1968 and the University of California, Berkeley in 1969 led to ethnic studies programs; Amy Uyematsu's 'The Emergence of Yellow Power' appeared in 1969; the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized for internment and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee.
stimulus.text:
In November 1968, students at San Francisco State University went on strike, demanding courses in Black, Latino, and Asian American history and culture. Similar strikes followed at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1969. The strikes led colleges to create ethnic studies programs.

In 1969, Amy Uyematsu wrote an essay, "The Emergence of Yellow Power," urging Asian Americans to examine their own conditions and fight injustice. Asian American activists also sought reparations for Japanese Americans forced into internment camps during World War II. In 1988, the federal government apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee.

stem: The 1988 apology and payments to Japanese American internees best show which of the following?

options.text: That the government admitted internment was wrong more than forty years later
That the government paid reparations before World War II had ended
options.misconception: The passage says the government apologized and paid in 1988, more than forty years after the war.

options.text: That Japanese Americans were never interned during World War II
options.misconception: The passage says Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps during World War II.

options.text: That the payments ended all debate about the internment
options.misconception: An apology and payment did not end all debate; the passage claims no such thing.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Japanese Americans were forced into camps during World War II, and in 1988 the federal government formally apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee.
rationales.B: The passage says the government apologized and paid in 1988, more than forty years after the war.
rationales.C: The passage says Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps during World War II.
rationales.D: An apology and payment did not end all debate, and the passage claims no such thing.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps during World War II.
2. Background: For decades the government offered no apology and no payment.
3. Background: In 1988, the Civil Liberties Act apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee.
4. That long wait shows redress can come a generation late, and still matter to the people who receive it.
Remember: A wrong can be admitted long after it happened, and the delay is part of the story.
